::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## The decision this serves
In three years a regulator asks which analysis produced the exposure–response
figure in the label, and whether it can be re-run. Everything in this lesson
exists so the answer is "yes, here" rather than an afternoon of archaeology.
:::

## 1. Why modelers resist this, and why they are wrong

The usual objections are real, and each has a short answer.

> *"My work isn't software."*

Your work is a pipeline that turns inputs into a number someone acts on. That
is exactly what version control was built for. The fact that some of the code is
a control stream and some of the output is a plot changes nothing.

> *"Our environment is validated and controlled."*

Validated environments control the *software*. They do not tell you which of
your fourteen model runs produced figure 12, why run 09 was abandoned, or what
changed between the dataset used for the interim and the final. That is your
problem, and git solves it.

> *"I use `run_final_v3_REALLY_final.mod`."*

Everyone did, once. The failure is not aesthetic: it loses the *reasoning*.
Filenames record that something changed; they never record why.

## 2. The minimum that actually works

Five commands cover ninety percent of a modeler's use. Learn these, ignore the
rest until you need it.

```bash
git init                    # once per project
git status                  # what have I changed?
git add file.qmd            # stage a specific change
git commit -m "message"     # record it, with the reason
git log --oneline           # what happened, in order
```

Add three more when you start collaborating:

```bash
git switch -c covariate-model   # work on a change without disturbing main
git diff                        # what exactly changed
git tag -a v1.0 -m "interim analysis dataset v2"   # mark a state you will be asked about
```

That is the whole toolkit. Branching strategies, rebasing and the rest are
software-engineering concerns you can pick up later, or never.

### Commit messages are the deliverable

The commit *message* is the part with lasting value, because it records the
thing no diff can show: **why**.

Weak: `updated model`.
Useful: `add allometric WT on CL/Q, exponents fixed at 0.75 — free estimation gave 0.93 (95% CI 0.57-1.30), too wide to support`.

Twenty of those and you have a reasoning log for the entire analysis, which is
what you will actually need when writing the report or answering a question at
a review meeting.

## 3. What goes in, and what stays out

| Commit | Never commit |
|---|---|
| Model code, control streams, scripts | Patient-level clinical data |
| The **assembly script** that builds the dataset | Anything under a confidentiality restriction |
| Configuration, environment lockfiles | Licence keys, credentials, licence servers |
| Small synthetic or public datasets | Large binary outputs that can be regenerated |
| The check battery from `S0-03` | Fitted objects of hundreds of megabytes |
| Report sources (`.qmd`, `.Rmd`) | Rendered PDFs regenerated on every build |

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
**Real clinical data does not go in a repository**, and certainly not a public
one — no exceptions, no "just for a moment", no private-repo reasoning. What
goes in is the *script* that builds the dataset from the controlled source, plus
a checksum of the dataset it produced. That gives you full traceability with no
patient data in version control, and it is the arrangement your data-governance
group will accept.
:::

## 4. A project layout that survives handover

```
compound-x-poppk/
├── README.md              # what this is, who owns it, how to run it
├── data/
│   ├── source/            # read-only, never edited, checksummed
│   └── derived/           # built by scripts/, gitignored
├── scripts/
│   ├── 01-assemble.R      # source -> analysis-ready
│   ├── 02-checks.R        # the S0-03 battery, fails loudly
│   └── 03-explore.R
├── models/
│   ├── run001/            # one directory per run, never overwritten
│   └── run002/
├── report/
│   └── poppk-report.qmd
├── renv.lock              # or uv.lock / requirements.txt
└── .gitignore
```

Four conventions carry most of the value:

1. **Numbered scripts that run in order.** Anyone can see the pipeline without
   reading the code.
2. **One directory per model run, never overwritten.** Disk is cheap;
   reconstructing run 7 is not.
3. **`data/source` is read-only.** Every derived file is regenerated by a
   script. If you cannot delete `data/derived` and rebuild it, the pipeline is
   incomplete.
4. **A README that names the owner and the run command.** Handover is the norm,
   not the exception.

## 5. Environments

Code without its environment is not reproducible. Pin it:

- **R:** `renv::init()`, then `renv::snapshot()`. Commit `renv.lock`.
- **Python:** `uv` or `pip-tools`; commit the lockfile, not a bare
  `requirements.txt` of unpinned names.
- **Either:** a container image for anything that must run identically in five
  years. This is what `S7` builds on.

The test is blunt and worth actually performing: **can a colleague clone the
repository and reproduce figure 3 on a clean machine?** Until you have watched
someone do it, you do not know.

## 6. The analysis dossier

Regulated work adds a documentation layer that git supports but does not
replace:

- **A run log** — every model run, its purpose, its outcome, and whether it fed
  a conclusion. Abandoned runs matter; "we tried that and it did not converge"
  is a finding.
- **An exclusion log** — every excluded subject or record, the reason, the
  decision-maker, the date.
- **Dataset versions**, with a checksum recorded per model run.
- **A tag at every milestone** — interim analysis, database lock, submission.
  `git tag` takes two seconds and turns "which version was that?" into a lookup.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
## Failure mode — reproducible in principle, not in fact
The most common reproducibility failure is not a missing file. It is a pipeline
that has only ever been run *forward*, incrementally, by the person who wrote
it, with a manual step nobody wrote down — a column renamed by hand, a row
deleted in a spreadsheet, a script run out of order once.

It reproduces perfectly on that person's machine and nowhere else, and this is
never discovered until they leave.

The only reliable defence is to **delete `data/derived`, clear the environment,
and run the pipeline end to end from a clean checkout**, on a schedule. Do it
monthly during an active analysis, and always before database lock. Put it in
continuous integration and the machine does it for you every time you push.
:::

## Check yourself

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 1. Why is committing the assembly script better than committing the dataset?
The script is small, diffable and reviewable — you can see exactly what changed
between versions, which you cannot do with a CSV. It contains no patient data,
so it can live wherever is convenient. And it forces the pipeline to be complete:
if the script does not fully build the dataset, the gap becomes visible
immediately rather than three years later. Record a checksum of the output
alongside it, and you have traceability without the data.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 2. Your organisation forbids git for validated analyses. What do you do?
Use it for everything *up to* the validated boundary — exploration, method
development, report drafting, the check battery — and follow the controlled
process for the final analysis. Then push for change with an argument the
quality group actually cares about: a git history is a stronger audit trail than
a directory of dated folders, because it is tamper-evident and records
intent. Most such prohibitions were written before anyone in the room had used
version control.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 3. How do you version a dataset that legitimately changes mid-analysis?
Version the dataset explicitly (`adppk_v1`, `adppk_v2`), record which version
each model run used, and never overwrite a version in place. Then diff them —
row counts, subject counts, and a summary of what changed — and write that diff
into the run log. A dataset that changes silently under a series of model runs
is one of the few defects that can invalidate an entire analysis after the fact.
:::

## Going further

- **Next:** [S0-06 · Reading a model report](../s0-06-reading-a-model-report/).
- **Builds on this:** `S7` — containers, workflow managers, and QC in a
  GxP-adjacent environment.
- **Reference:** any short git tutorial for the mechanics; the value of this
  lesson is in the conventions, not the commands.

*Seen in the wild:* a submission question asked why two exposure summaries in
different documents disagreed in the third significant figure. The answer took
three weeks to establish, and turned out to be two dataset versions differing by
one excluded subject. With tagged datasets and a run log it would have taken ten
minutes.
